findings.title: Unilateral credit line reduction with termination
findings.triggered_by: By giving you written notice, we may reduce your Credit Line from time to time, or, with good cause, revoke your card and terminate this Agreement.
findings.description: Unilateral credit line reduction with termination
findings.search_query_used: credit card change in terms unilateral modification account cancellation

precedents.case_name: Qualls v. Wright Patt Credit Union

findings.plain_language_explanation: The bank can cut your credit limit or cancel your card anytime with just a written notice. They don't need your permission or a serious reason.
findings.user_impact: If you carry a balance, sudden credit cuts could push you over limit with fees and hurt your score.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: Bank reduces your $5,000 limit to $2,000 while you owe $3,500. You're now over limit, facing penalty fees, higher interest rates, and credit score damage.

recommended_actions.action: Pay down existing balances below 30% of current limits before any changes
Apply for a backup credit card from different bank as emergency option
Set up account alerts to monitor any credit limit changes immediately
recommended_actions.contact: Card issuer online banking or app

findings.title: Vague 'good cause' termination standard
findings.triggered_by: Good cause includes your failure to comply with this Agreement, our adverse reevaluation of your creditworthiness or your use of this card in furtherance of any purpose deemed to be illegal under state or federal law.
findings.search_query_used: credit card change in terms unilateral modification account cancellation

precedents.case_name: Canteen v. Charlotte Metro Credit Union

findings.plain_language_explanation: The bank can close your credit card account for 'good cause' but doesn't clearly define what that means, giving them too much power to cancel anytime.
findings.user_impact: As a retiree who carries a balance, your card could be canceled unexpectedly, hurting your credit score.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: Bank suddenly closes your account while you have a balance, forcing immediate payment you can't afford and damaging your credit score when you're on fixed retirement income.

recommended_actions.action: Ask the bank to define 'good cause' in writing before signing
Shop for cards with clearer termination terms

findings.title: Balance transfers treated as cash advances
findings.triggered_by: Balances you transfer from other creditors will be treated as cash advances for the purpose of this agreement and will be subject to your standard cash advance APR unless a promotional APR applies.
findings.description: Balance transfers treated as cash advances
findings.search_query_used: credit card fee disclosure TILA Truth in Lending hidden fees
findings.plain_language_explanation: Balance transfers from other credit cards will be charged the higher cash advance rate instead of the regular purchase rate, making debt consolidation expensive.
findings.user_impact: Your transferred balances will have higher interest rates, increasing monthly payments on fixed income.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: Transferring $5,000 in debt could cost an extra $50-100 monthly in interest charges, straining your retirement budget and making debt payoff much harder.

recommended_actions.action: Ask for written confirmation of balance transfer APR before signing
Compare with other cards offering true balance transfer rates
Consider debt counseling for retirement-friendly options

findings.title: Unilateral payment allocation discretion
findings.triggered_by: Subject to applicable law, your payments may be applied to what you owe the Credit Union in any manner the Credit Union chooses.
findings.description: Credit union has discretion to apply payments in manner that may not benefit consumer

precedents.case_name: Connie Edwards v. Your Credit, Inc.

findings.plain_language_explanation: The credit union can decide how to apply your payments without your input. They might put money toward fees first instead of your balance.
findings.user_impact: Your payments may not reduce your debt as expected, keeping you in debt longer with more fees.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: You make payments thinking they'll reduce your main balance, but the credit union applies them to fees and interest first, keeping your debt high and costing you more money.

recommended_actions.action: Ask the credit union to explain their payment allocation policy in writing before signing
recommended_actions.contact: Credit union loan officer or member services

recommended_actions.action: Request they agree to apply payments to highest interest debt first
Consider shopping with other credit unions that offer clearer payment terms

findings.title: Balance becomes immediately due on termination
findings.triggered_by: Upon revocation of your card any outstanding balance and FINANCE CHARGE shall immediately become due and payable under the terms of this Agreement.
findings.description: Entire balance acceleration can create financial hardship for elderly consumers on fixed income
findings.search_query_used: upon revocation your card outstanding balance finance charge credit card consumer rights
findings.plain_language_explanation: If the credit card company cancels your card for any reason, you must pay back everything you owe right away - no more monthly payments allowed.
findings.user_impact: On fixed retirement income, you'd need to pay your full balance at once instead of monthly payments.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: Card gets canceled due to late payment or credit changes. With limited retirement income, you can't pay the full balance immediately, leading to collections and damaged credit.

recommended_actions.action: Ask the lender to modify this clause to allow reasonable payment arrangements even after cancellation
Consider cards with more consumer-friendly terms that don't require immediate full payment
recommended_actions.contact: Other credit card companies or credit union

recommended_actions.action: Keep emergency savings equal to your credit card balance to avoid payment problems

findings.plain_language_explanation: When you move debt from one card to this one, you lose the time to pay new purchases without interest. You'll pay interest right away on new buys.
findings.user_impact: Since you carry balances, new purchases will cost more due to immediate interest charges.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: You transfer $3,000 debt, then buy $500 groceries. Instead of 25 days to pay without interest, you immediately owe interest on the $500 at 24% APR - costing extra $10/month.

Ask card company to confirm grace period terms before transferring

findings.plain_language_explanation: Even if you pay part of what you owe or write 'paid in full' on a check, the lender can still demand the full amount and take collection actions.
findings.user_impact: You might think partial payments settle your debt, but the lender can still sue or collect.
findings.estimated_risk_scenario: You send a partial payment thinking it settles the debt, but the lender accepts it and still pursues you for the remaining balance, potentially leading to lawsuits or damage to credit.

Consult with a consumer attorney about debt settlement rights
